transcript:
Meeting header: 
Date: 2026-11-20 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Jasmine Lee (Redwood AE), Carlos Mendes (Redwood SE), Tom Keller (Acme - CTO), Priya Sharma (Acme - Lead Eng), Evan Liu (Acme - Eng)

[00:00] Jasmine: Hey everyone, thanks for making time. I'm Jasmine from Redwood, this is Carlos, our solutions engineer. Quick agenda SDK quickstart, auth and env setup, a quick Console tour for Optimize, then Q&A and next steps.
[00:18] Tom: Great, thanks. We're mostly concerned with getting a dev-friendly SDK flow for both Python and TypeScript and making sure auth fits into our CI and SSO properties.
[00:32] Carlos: Perfect. We'll show the python quickstart first, then TS. Quick note, some of the package names in early docs we've seen a few folks type in redwood-sdk vs redwood-inference, so watch for that.
[00:45] Priya: Yeah we ran into that actually when we tried the public repo little mismatch.
[00:52] Carlos: Cool. So python, simplest path, pip install redwood-inference (or use our wheel), set env var REDWOOD_API_KEY, then from redwood import Client, resp = client.generate(prompt=...) and you'll get a streaming iterator if you set stream=True.
[01:10] Evan: Is the streaming over SSE or web sockets in python?
[01:14] Carlos: The python SDK uses chunked HTTP streaming, similar to SSE, and the TS SDK supports WebSocket and event-source flavors depending on the environment. There's an example in the quickstart.
[01:28] Tom: For auth we want to avoid long-lived keys in build agents, is there a recommended pattern?
[01:33] Jasmine: Yes, two common patterns: 1) Short-lived API keys issued via your identity provider  we support SSO/SAML provisioning and short lived token exchange; 2) Use a service account + KMS encryption for on-prem/private setups. For CI specifically, the recommended is ephemeral tokens minted by your IDP and stored in CI secrets for the job lifetime.
[01:55] Priya: How does the token rotation work do you have an endpoint?
[01:59] Carlos: We expose a token exchange endpoint in Private deployments; for hosted, you can integrate with our SSO + OIDC flow and we support SCIM user provisioning. Some customers just rotate keys weekly via scripts, others use a vault.
[02:12] Tom: Ok. Can we see a concrete env example?
[02:15] Carlos: Yep. In Python you do: export REDWOOD_API_KEY=sk_live_xxx (we usually advise not to store literal in repo). Or in .env: REDWOOD_API_KEY=sk_live_xxx and then pipenv or dotenv. For TypeScript: in node you might do process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY or use the @redwood/inference client which will check process.env and fall back to well-known locations.
[02:40] Evan: Are there first-class CI examples for GitHub Actions?
[02:42] Carlos: Yes, our quickstart repo includes a .github/workflows/ci.yml that reads the key from secrets and runs a small smoke test. We'll share that link.
[02:52] Tom: How about the console can product managers inspect usage and route to different models?
[02:56] Jasmine: Yup. Quick tour now. Carlos?
[03:00] Carlos: (screenshare) Console > Projects > Routes  you can pin a route to a model family, add fallbacks, and set autoscale. Optimize tab gives batching and quantization recommendations based on observed request size and latency. For example, for Acme's 512-token median, Optimize suggests medium batching with kv cache on to reduce cost by ~20%. (note: suggestion is sample data)
[03:28] Priya: Is kv cache safe for multi-tenant traffic?
[03:31] Carlos: Yes; we partition cache per-customer or per-route; on Dedicated/Private you control the instance boundaries.
[03:39] Tom: For the POC we'll likely want dedicated capacity but maybe start on hosted. Performance discipline is key  can you help run a benchmark with our payloads?
[03:49] Jasmine: Absolutely. If you can share sample prompts and qps, Carlos will run a 1-hour benchmark and share 50/95/99 pct latencies and tokens/sec.
[04:00] Evan: Cool. About the SDK code samples any differences in how you handle function calling or structured output?
[04:06] Carlos: Function calling is supported in both SDKs in TS you'll get typed callbacks and we also provide a helpers package for JSON schema parsing. The python client returns a parsed object if content-type json is detected. Small caveat: the transcription in older docs used to say function-calling is only in TS, that's not accurate, both are supported.
[04:31] Priya: Are there known gotchas on types for TypeScript?
[04:34] Carlos: Watch your tsconfig targeting  older node targets may need polyfills for fetch/websocket; we have a small adapter file in the quickstart called fetch-adapter.ts.
[04:44] Tom: One of our security folks asked about audit logs and traceability  do you capture per request audit logs and user identity?
[04:51] Jasmine: Yes, we log request metadata, model version, route, and identity token when SSO is enabled. For Private deployments you can push logs to your ELK or S3. We'll include the audit log schema in the docs.
[05:05] Priya: KMS integration  if we use our key, is that supported?
[05:08] Carlos: Yes, for Private deployments we support customer-managed keys (KMS/HSM). For hosted we offer envelope encryption where you can manage the root key via a supported KMS provider. We'll attach the integration note.
[05:20] Evan: About quickstarts can you walk through a minimal Python example on the call?
[05:24] Carlos: Sure. (typing) Example:

# python quickstart snippet (spoken)
from redwood import Client
client = Client(api_key=os.environ.get('REDWOOD_API_KEY'))
resp = client.generate(prompt='Summarize this...')
for chunk in resp.stream():
    print(chunk.text, end='')

[05:50] Priya: That looks straightforward. For TypeScript?
[05:54] Carlos: TS quickstart: npm install @redwood/inference
import Redwood from '@redwood/inference'
const client = new Redwood.Client({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY })
const stream = client.generateStream({ prompt: 'Summarize...' })
stream.on('data', chunk => console.log(chunk.text))

[06:14] Tom: We saw code that used client.createCompletion is that an alias?
[06:18] Carlos: Yes, createCompletion is kept for compatibility; generate and generateStream are the recommended modern names.
[06:24] Jasmine: Quick note on package naming again the quickstart repo has both python and ts folders. We'll send the repo link after the call.
[06:32] Evan: For our POC, we need an end-to-end example of auth: SSO -> mint short lived token -> CI uses token. Is that documented?
[06:40] Carlos: We have a flow doc and a sample script that uses OIDC code flow to mint a service token, then exchanges for a short-lived key. We'll include a sample GitHub Actions job that demonstrates exchange.
[06:51] Priya: Any rate limit considerations for bursty traffic? We have spikes to 200 qps during batch jobs.
[06:57] Carlos: For that scale, Dedicated is recommended. Hosted can do burst but Dedicated gives predictable throughput and isolation. Also use batching to smooth bursts; Optimize can suggest batching window and batch size.
[07:10] Tom: Security review question what compliance docs can we share?
[07:13] Jasmine: SOC2 Type II and ISO/IEC are available; we'll send the artifacts and the security questionnaire answers. For Private deployments we can sign custom contracts for data residency.
[07:24] Evan: Will you share the network diagram for Private?
[07:27] Jasmine: Yes, Carlos will attach standard network config and customer-specific diagram templates.
[07:32] (brief pause while Carlos toggles screenshare)
[07:40] Carlos: Back to SDK  small demo of local env: .env with REDWOOD_API_KEY, python venv, pip install, run smoke test. Then a sample GitHub Actions snippet where you set secrets.REDWOOD_API_KEY and call the smoke test.
[07:56] Priya: How is usage metered? Token count? Request counts?
[08:00] Jasmine: Primary metering is per-token for generation and per-embedding unit for embeddings. Console breaks down token-level cost by route and model, so you can see top spenders.
[08:12] Tom: For embeddings, do you have batch endpoints? We plan a large reindexing job.
[08:17] Carlos: Yes, batch embeddings API and we also recommend using our dedup cache to lower costs. For big jobs, Dedicated with heavy I/O config is recommended.
[08:27] Priya: One more on SDK: error handling patterns what errors do we expose?
[08:31] Carlos: HTTP 429 for rate limits, 5xx for infra, and rich error payloads in JSON with retriable flag. The client exposes retries by default with exponential backoff. We surfaced idempotency keys for safety in record style workloads.
[08:48] Evan: Does the TS client play nice in edge runtimes? We use Cloudflare Workers for some functions.
[08:53] Carlos: Edge support is experimental but we have an adapter for fetch-only runtimes. Some features like websocket streaming are limited in pure edge environments. We'll share the compatibility table.
[09:05] Tom: Ok, let's talk next steps we want pricing, SOC2 docs, and a POC plan.
[09:10] Jasmine: We'll do that: pricing + security docs by Tuesday, Carlos will prepare the quickstart repo and benchmark script, and we'll schedule a POC kickoff for week of 11/30.
[09:21] Priya: POC scope can we get a 2-week POC that includes a small dedicated pool and 1-hour benchmark?
[09:27] Jasmine: Absolutely, we'll propose a POC scope and cost. If you'd like, we can start on hosted then migrate to a small dedicated pool for the benchmark.
[09:36] Tom: That would work. Also please include a checklist of what we need to provide (prompts, traffic profiles, SSO contacts).
[09:43] Jasmine: Will do.
[09:46] Evan: Couple of micro-notes we noticed occasional transcription mismatch in docs: redwood console vs redwood consolee tiny but might confuse.
[09:54] Carlos: Good catch, we'll clean that up in the quickstart README.
[09:58] Jasmine: Anything else?
[10:00] Priya: Nothing else from us. Thanks for the walkthrough.
[10:03] Jasmine: Recap and next steps: 1) Jasmine send pricing + SOC2 + network diagram; 2) Carlos share quickstart repo and TS/py snippets and benchmark script; 3) Customer to share traffic/profile; 4) Schedule POC kickoff week of 11/30.
[10:20] Tom: Sounds good. Thanks.
[10:22] (call ends)

Notes on transcript quality: occasional mis-hearings, package names and function names called out as approximate. Links referenced quickstart repo, security docs, benchmark spreadsheet will be sent as follow-ups.
